newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean president under siege as minister quits.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean president under siege as minister quits.

text.p: A South Korean loans scandal on Wednesday threatened to engulf President Kim Young-sam in an election year as the home minister quit and another of Kim's trusted associates was grilled by prosecutors.
Home Affairs Minister Kim Woo-suk became the first cabinet casualty of the scandal, which involves loans to failed Hanbo Steel Co and is reaching deeper into Kim's inner sanctum.
The prime minister indicated he, too, was willing to resign amid media speculation that the whole cabinet would have to go.
The home minister is being questioned by state prosecutors on suspicion of taking kickbacks but has not been charged with any wrongdoing.
Also being questioned was ruling New Korea Party legislator Hwang Byung-tai, who heads the powerful finance and economy committee in parliament.
Hwang and the home minister are key members of the so-called "Minju" faction of Kim loyalists that engineered his rise to the presidential Blue House in 1993.

On Tuesday prosecutors arrested another veteran member of Kim's personal entourage, Hong In-gil, and Chung Jae-chull, the highest-ranking official in the ruling New Korea Party after the president and the party chairman.
Both have been charged with accepting kickbacks in connection with loans to Hanbo.

In an apparent bid to limit the damage to the ruling party ahead of presidential polls in December, Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung made known he was prepared to carry the blame for one of South Korea's biggest bankruptcies now turning into a political crisis for the president.
"He is willing (to resign)," an official in Lee's office said. "But it's up to the president."

Although President Kim personally ordered an investigation into how Hanbo Steel leveraged its net worth of $300 million to secure $6 billion in loans, and has openly called it a graft case, his credibility is now on the line.
One by one, Kim's trusted advisers -- his top lieutenants in a fight against corruption that has defined his presidency -- are being buried by sleaze.
The home affairs minister was the third cabinet member to depart in less than six months under a corruption cloud.
Yonhap news agency said "a mass resignation of the entire cabinet could follow the conclusion of the Hanbo investigation."
Kim cannot run for a second term in office, but with scandal swirling closer to him and his party's power centre he will have less room to maneuver as he seeks to anoint a successor.
Already, there are signs of factional in-fighting in the ruling camp as presidential candidates jockey for position.

The aspirations of party chairman Lee Hong-koo are thought to have been mortally wounded by a botched effort last year to revise the country's labour law, a fiasco that led to almost one month of wildcat strikes.
Prosecutors on Wednesday also grilled Kwon Roh-kap, a top aide to main opposition leader Kim Dae-jung.
Newspaper editorials and analysts said the Hanbo probe had so far only touched the surface of the scandal.
"The investigation into the political circle touched only the outer branches of the Hanbo incident," the Hankook Ilbo newspaper said in an editorial.
Hanbo Group founder Chung Tae-soo has been arrested on charges of fraud and other violations. Two bankers have also been arrested on bribery charges.

"The Hanbo scandal has again highlighted the corrupt alliance between politics and business," an Asian diplomat said. "Many South Koreans believe the prosecution has shed light on only the tip of a sleazy iceberg."
